newsitem.title: UK: UK RATE VIEWS POLARISED AFTER INFLATION REPORT.
newsitem.headline: UK RATE VIEWS POLARISED AFTER INFLATION REPORT.

text.p: The pause signalled by the Bank of England in the recent pattern of monthly hikes in official interest rates has polarised economist views on the timing and direction of the next move.

Interest rate bears said on Wednesday the rate rise respite could be as little as two months whilst the bulls argue rates have already peaked at their current level of 7.0 percent and the next move will be downwards.

The lack of a consensus is unsurprising given that Mervyn King, chief economist at the Bank of England and a key member of the central bank's interest rate setting Monetary Policy Committee, is himself uncertain how long the pause will last.
King told reporters that the duration "will depend on what information comes in." Moreover, he added that the committee had not decided that the next move in interest rates would be up.
In the bear camp, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr argues that the market view suggested by short sterling, that rates are close to their peak, is dangerously complacent.

"There's a risk they could go up even before November. The Bank has given us several pointers -- average earnings, excessive credit and money growth -- and our view is that these will remain strong, forcing them to raise rates again."
Barr sees official rates, currently at 7.0 percent, peaking at 8.0 percent in the second quarter of next year as the central bank struggles to keep inflation to its 2.5 percent target level.
At the other extreme, UBS economist Andrew Cates and Nikko economist Julian Jessop say the next move could be down.

"With most forward looking survey indicators of both the manufacturing and service sectors suggesting that the economy is already starting to slow, we believe that base rates are likely to remain unchanged for the rest of this year," said UBS's Cates.

"Base rates are more likely to be reduced in the early half of 1998 than to be raised," he said, arguing that the boost to consumer spending power from building society windfall payments will start to unwind.

Whilst Nikko's Jessop says that the Bank may be over bearish in its assessment of the prospects for sterling and this could mean official rates are set to fall. "If the next move in interest rates is indeed down, excessive sterling strength on European Monetary Union worries is the most likely trigger," he said.
The Bank said it expected sterling to fall to around 90.0 on the effective exchange rate index in two years time, from 100.8 now, limiting its deflationary impact on the economy.

Jessop added that the central bank's assessment of the economy was confusing because it argued that the impact of sterling's current effect should be treated as a one-off whilst the one-off windfall payments are considered reason enough to still be thinking of raising rates.
"The Bank almost seems to be looking for bad news, though some would see this as what a good central bank should do," he said.

In the moderate camp on rates, Goldman Sachs UK economist David Walton agrees with the central bank's view of a gradual decline in sterling and sees a peak in rates of 7.5 percent in the spring of 1998.

He sees the next increase at the November 5-6 monthly monetary meeting and says this will enable the next quarterly inflation report, due November 12, to say that Britain is still on course to hit its inflation target even if the data over the next few months remain strong.

"If the data are not moving the way they expect then rates will go up in November and I don't think people should take it for granted that the rise will be a quarter point. They've made it clear that 1/2 point rises are a possibility," he said.
